title.rendered: Immuun checkpoint remmers in urologische kankers

content.rendered:
In European Urology Systematic Review of Immune Checkpoint Inhibition in Urological Cancers, een onderzoek vanuit DUOS ziekenhuis ErasmusMC Kankerinstituut dat tevens leidde tot het onderstaande persbericht van Reuters Health.

NEW YORK (Reuters Health) – In patients with advanced urothelial cell and renal cell cancers, immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are more effective and safer than conventional second-line treatment, a new systematic review from The Netherlands reports.

Immune checkpoint inhibitors can reactivate the immune system against tumor cells and improve clinical outcomes in patients with advanced and metastatic urological cancers, the authors wrote. In second-line settings, pembrolizumab and nivolumab are safe and confer survival benefit in advanced urothelial cell and renal cell cancer, respectively.

“We provide a comprehensive overview of the efficacy and safety of immune checkpoint inhibitors in urological cancer patients. As second-line treatment, immune checkpoint inhibitors have expanded the treatment options for patients with advanced urothelial and renal cell cancer,” coauthor Dr. Astrid A. M. van der Veldt of Erasmus Medical Center Cancer Institute in Rotterdam, The Netherlands, told Reuters Health. “These clinical findings are in line with previously published data on mutational burden showing that tumors with a high mutational load (urothelial cell cancer) are more sensitive to checkpoint blockade than tumors with a low mutational load (prostate cancer),” she said in an email.

As reported online June 20 in European Urology, Dr. van der Veldt and her colleagues searched the standard large medical databases through spring 2017 for randomized clinical trials, and they reviewed the literature on the efficacy and safety of ICIs in patients with advanced and metastatic prostate cancer, renal cell cancer (RCC) and urothelial cell cancer (UCC). They selected six randomized controlled trials.

In platinum-pretreated UCC, the efficacy of pembrolizumab was superior to chemotherapy. Patients lived longer, with a median overall survival of 10.3 vs 7.4 months; they also had an objective response rate of 21.1% vs 11.4% (p=0.001), and a lower adverse event rate of 60.9% vs 90.2%, respectively. Three randomized controlled trials evaluated the safety and efficacy of nivolumab in advanced renal cell cancer. The median overall survival, 25.0 vs 19.6 months, and the objective response rates, 25% vs 5%, were higher in patients treated with nivolumab compared with second-line everolimus. All three studies reported a favorable safety profile for nivolumab.

In patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, the two randomized controlled trials that were identified did not show significant benefits for ipilimumab over placebo. No conclusive association was found between programmed cell death receptor ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression in tumor tissue and clinical outcome during pembrolizumab and nivolumab treatment for UCC and RCC, respectively. Dr. Van der Veldt said the selection of only high-level evidence clinical trials (phase III trials) is a strength of the study.

Dr. Jorge Ramos of the University of Washington in Seattle and Seattle Cancer Care Alliance, said in an email, “These findings were not surprising. This study compiled previously published data. In addition to the studies discussed in the article, checkpoint inhibitors have been shown to improve outcomes and are FDA approved across a wide range of malignancies including melanoma, head and neck cancer, certain types of lung cancer, and Hodgkin lymphoma.” Dr. Ramos, who was not involved in the study, told Reuters Health that synthesizing the data for ICIs in urological cancers is beneficial.
“An interesting point is that, although ipilimumab did not demonstrate improved outcomes in prostate cancer in the studies described in the article, it does not mean that checkpoint inhibitors will not work in prostate cancer. In other malignancies, PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors have been shown to work better than ipilimumab (a CTLA-4 inhibitor). Therefore, PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors should still be investigated in prostate cancer,” he said. He added that “a limitation of the study is that the inclusion and exclusion criteria were a little too stringent. The main unanswered question is that we know that these drugs work in later stages of disease, but are they as effective in earlier stages, such as in patients with newly diagnosed metastatic cancer or in patients with localized disease who are planning to undergo surgery for their cancer?” he asked.

“PD-L1 expression has yet to be shown to be a reliable marker of response to PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors. There are patients who do not have significant PD-L1 expression on biopsy who respond to PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors. Therefore, in urological cancers, they should not be used to decide whether to treat patients with PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors. More studies are necessary to identify markers that select patients who are more likely to respond to treatment,” Dr. Ramos said.

Dr. Van der Veldt told Reuters Health that her group’s future research plans include combination therapies, treatment with ICIs for earlier disease stages, and the development of tools to better select patients for ICI treatment.
